newsitem.title: USA: NYS Gov hedges optimism over NYC finance agency.
newsitem.headline: NYS Gov hedges optimism over NYC finance agency.

text.p: New York State Gov George Pataki on Monday hedged optimistic comments about how close Albany and New York City lawmakers were to reaching an agreement on a new finance authority for the city.

"We are very close to an agreement on the Infrastructure Finance Authority, that should be passing, I would hope, in the near future, but again that was something we had essentially agreement on in December," Pataki told reporters in Albany.

He was referring to a plan to let the city sidestep a state-imposed debt cap by creating a new borrowing arm that could sell up to $7.5 billion of bonds over four years for its schools and infrastructure. That agreement, along with a plan to extend the 12.5 percent personal income tax surcharge, collapsed in a special, December legislative session.

The legislature's failure to approve the the new measures was a major blow to the city as it collects about $450 million to $500 million from the personal income tax surcharge, which expired at the end of 1996. And the city is expected to hit its debt ceiling about one month before the start of its 1998 fiscal year on July 1.
New York City sources had said the two sides were close to agreement over the new finance authority and were expected to announce a deal as soon as early this week.
Spokesmen for the Guiliani Administration, the Senate Majoity Leader and the Assembly Speaker were not immediately available to comment.
The sources, who declined to be named, added that they knew of no breakthrough efforts to resolve differences over extending the personal income tax surcharge.

Pataki said he did not know what impact a lawsuit filed last Friday by Staten Island Borough President Guy Molinari, who wants to stop the state from collecting the tax because it has expired, would have on the issue.

The state has kept assessing the tax for the city, which helps pay for more police officers. A two-year preliminary agreement reached in December but never concluded was also expected to provide $550 million for school construction.

In his suit, which was filed in Albany in New York State Suprement Court, Molinari argued that it was illegal to continue to collect the tax, which when it was imposed was expected to be a temporary measure, after it expired.
"The government should obey the laws it passes and uphold the commitments it makes," he said, in prepared remarks.
A spokesman for Molinari noted the legislator had approved the tax when it first was put in place, adding he had asked that the case be heard on March 7.

The governor, evidently responding to criticism about the state's failure last July to approve a budget on time, a logjam that in part was blamed on his willingness to hold up the process to hammer out a pact that would sharply reduce the cost of workers' compensation insurance, reiterated his support for the $3.4 billion school tax relief program he proposed.
He added that while the plan "to me, obviously is very, very important," no issues could not be negotiated.
